items.e: We may only partake of the produce of the Sabbatical year as long as that species is found in the field. [This is derived from Leviticus 25:7]: "For the animal and the beast in your land will be all the produce to eat." [Implied is that] as long as a beast [can be] eating from this species in the field, one may eat from [what he has collected] at home. When there is no longer any [of that species] for the beast to eat in the field, one is obligated to remove that species from his home. This is the obligation of biyur which applies to the produce of the Sabbatical year.

What is implied? If a person has dried figs at home, he may partake of them as long as there are figs on the trees in the field. When there are no longer figs in the field, it is forbidden for him to partake of the figs he has at home and he must instead remove them.

If he had a large amount of produce, he should distribute a quantity that can be eaten in three meals to every person [he desires]. It is forbidden - both for the rich and the poor - to partake of it after the time of biyur . If he is not able to find people to eat at the time of biyur , he should burn it with fire or cast it into Mediterranean Sea, or destroy it through any other means.

If one had raisins from the Sabbatical year and there were no longer any grapes left in the fields, the gardens, and the orchards which are ownerless, even though there are still grapes on the vines in the courtyards, he may not partake of the raisins because of the grapes in the courtyard, because they are not accessible to a wild beast. If, however, there are very firm grapes that do not mature until the end of the year [still growing in the field], one may partake of the raisins [he has stored] because of them. Similar laws apply in all analogous instances.

When a tree produces fruit twice a year and one still possesses fruit from its first crop, he may partake of it as long as the second crop is still in the field. For [the requirement that] this species be [available] in the field [is met]. We do not, however, [continue to] partake [of stored fruit] because of fruit that grows in the fall, because it is considered as the produce of a different year.

When a person pickles three types of produce in one barrel, if one of these types of produce is no longer available in the field, that type of produce should be removed from the barrel. If he began partaking of [the pickled produce], the entire [mixture] is considered as having been removed. Just as one is obligated to remove food [stored for] human consumption, so too, must he remove animal fodder from his home and he may no longer feed it to an animal if that type of produce is no longer available in the field.

Just as one must remove the produce of the Sabbatical year, so too, one must remove the money [received in exchange for it]. What is implied? One sold pomegranates of the Sabbatical year and used the money received in return for them [to purchase] food. When there are no longer any pomegranates on the trees in the field, but he remains in possession of the money he received for selling them, he is obligated to remove it from his possession.

What should he do? He should purchase food with this money and distribute it, [providing] three meals to every person [he desires]. Alternatively, if he does not find people to partake of such food, he should cast the money into the Mediterranean Sea.

[ Eretz Yisrael is divided into] three lands [with regard to the obligation of] biyur : a) the entire land of Yehudah, its mountainous portion, its plain, and its valley, is all one region. b) the entire [West] Bank of the Jordan, [including] the plain of Lod, the mountains [around] the plain of Lod, [the area of] Beit Choron, with the sea, is all one region; and c) the entire Galilee, the upper [Galilee], the lower [Galilee], and the area of Tiberias, is one region. In each of these three regions, one may partake [of a species of produce stored at home] until the last [traces of that produce] cease [to exist in the entire region's fields].

What is implied? If one possesses produce in the land of Yehudah, one may partake of it as long as this species is found [in the fields of] the entire land of Yehudah. Similar laws apply if he possesses produce from the Galilee or from the [West] Bank of the Jordan.

These three regions are considered as one entity with regard to carobs, olives, and dates. One may eat dates [throughout Eretz Yisrael ] until the last dates are no longer available in Tzo'ar. From when are they no longer available? Purim. We may eat olives until Shavuot and grapes until Pesach of the eighth year. Dried figs may be eaten until Chanukah.

When a person transports produce of the Sabbatical year from a region in which it is no longer available [in the field] to a region where it is available, or from a region where it is available to a region in which it is no longer available, he is obligated in biyur . [The rationale is that] we place upon him the stringencies of the place from which he departed and those of the place to which he journeyed. When the produce of Eretz Yisrael has been brought to the Diaspora, it should be destroyed in its place. It should not be transported from one place to another.

A great general principle was stated with regard to [the produce of] the Sabbatical year: Whenever [produce] is [used as] food for humans, animal fodder, or as one of the dyes, if it will not be maintained in the earth, the laws of the Sabbatical year apply to it and to money received for it and the requirements of biyur apply to it and to money received for it, e.g., the leaves of wild onions, mint, and endives, are considered as food for humans, brambles and thorn are considered as animal fodder, and woad and safflower are considered as dyes. If the species is maintained in the earth, e.g., madder and dyer's rocket from the dyes, even though the laws of the Sabbatical year apply to it and to money received for it. The requirements of biyur do not apply to it or to money received for it, because it is maintained in the earth. Instead, one may benefit from it and use it as dye until Rosh HaShanah.

Whenever a plant is not set aside to be [used as] food for humans, animal fodder, or as one of the dyes, since it is not used as kindling fuel, the laws of the Sabbatical year apply to it and to money received for it, but the requirements of biyur do not apply to it or to those monies. [This applies] even if it will not be maintained in the earth. Instead, we may benefit from it and the money received for it until Rosh HaShanah. Examples [of this category include] the roots of wild onions and mint and the scorpion-like herb.

The laws of the Sabbatical year apply to the peels and the buds of pomegranates, the shells of nuts, and the seeds [of other fruits] and to the money received for them, but the requirements of biyur do not apply to them or to those monies. The laws of the Sabbatical year apply to the tips of the branches of grape vines and carob trees and to the money received for them, as do the requirements of biyur . The laws of the Sabbatical year apply to the tips of the branches of the evergreen oak, the pistachio tree, and the box thorn bush and to the money received for them, but the requirements of biyur do not apply to them. The requirement of biyur does apply to their leaves.

When is the time for biyur ? For leaves, it is when they wither and fall from the tree. The leaves of olive trees, reeds, and carob trees do not have a time of biyur , because they never wither and fall away.

Until when does a person have the license to gather fresh grass in the Sabbatical year? Until the bitter [apples] become dried out. He may gather dried grasses until the second rains of the eighth year.
Until when are the poor permitted to enter the orchards in the eighth year to gather the fruits of the Sabbatical year? Until the second rains descend.

The laws of the Sabbatical year apply to roses, cloves, and chestnuts and to the money received for them. The laws of the Sabbatical year do not apply to balsam sap that flows from trees, from their leaves, and their roots. They do apply to [sap] that flows from underdeveloped berries and the money received for it.

When does the above apply? When the tree produces edible fruit. If, however, the tree is not fruitbearing, the sap that flows from its leaves and roots is considered as its fruit and the laws of the Sabbatical year apply to it and to the money received for it.

When a person pickles a rose from the Sabbatical year in the oil of the sixth year, he may gather the rose and it is permitted [to use] the oil [in an ordinary manner]. If he pickles [a rose] in the oil of the eighth year, he is obligated to perform biyur with the oil. [The rationale is] at that time, the rose is dry and the obligation of biyur has already fallen upon it.

When carobs of the Sabbatical year were left to soak in the wine of the sixth year or in the wine of the eighth year, biyur must be performed with the wine, because it has absorbed the flavor of the produce of the Sabbatical year. This is the general principle: When the produce of the Sabbatical year becomes mixed with other produce of the same species, even the slightest amount [causes the entire mixture to be considered as the produce of the Sabbatical year]. When it becomes mixed with other species, [the ruling depends on whether it has] imparted its flavor [or not].
